summary: The abdomen in various species, including ferrets and humans, presents several clinical and histopathological findings. Ectopic adrenocortical tissue is commonly found in ferrets [C1:S1|PMC7149534]. Cardiomyopathy is also prevalent in ferrets and southern sea otters [C1:S3|PMC7149534]. In pediatric renal tumors, the involvement of abdominal or pelvic lymph nodes is a criterion for local stage III [C1:S9|PMC12232243], and residual non-haematogenous tumors confined to the abdomen are classified as COG local stage III [C1:S10|PMC12232243; C2:S1|PMC12232243]. Tumor implants can be found anywhere in the abdomen [C2:S3|PMC12232243]. In humans, a case study describes a 64-year-old male with a rash on his abdomen, which extended to the mid-anterior region [C2:S5|PMC4965535; C2:S6|PMC4965535]. A skin biopsy revealed nonspecific reactive changes [C2:S7|PMC4965535], and sonography was used to rule out distant metastasis [C2:S8|PMC11674806]. Histopathologically, Vitamin E deficiency in mustelids leads to significant changes, including adipocyte necrosis [C1:S2|PMC7149534], and inflammatory bowel disease is marked by lymphocyte infiltration and epithelial damage [C1:S4|PMC7149534].
